podcast.title: Lawsuit Against Sting (2025)
podcast.body: In 2025, Stuart Copeland, along with Andy Summers, sued Sting for arranger's fees they claim they are owed for "Every Breath You Take," arguing that his "cracking snare drum rhythm" was vital to the song's distinctive sound and enduring popularity. "Stings to police bandmates, guitarist Andy Summers and drummer Stuart Copeland have sued Sting for what they say they are owed for a ranger's fees on every breath you take."

podcast.body: When The Police's first album, *Outlandos d'Amour*, was released in 1978, Stuart Copeland was 26 years old, also older than many of their punk and new wave contemporaries. "Stuart Copeland was 26."

podcast.title: Brother's Role in Music Industry
podcast.body: His brother, Miles Copeland III, was an emerging music manager who would go on to establish the indie label IRS Records, which signed bands such as The Go-Go's and R.E.M. "Stuart's brother, Miles Copeland III, was a budding music manager who would go on to launch the indie label, IRS Records, which signed the Go-Go's and REM."

podcast.title: Contribution to "Every Breath You Take"
podcast.body: Stuart Copeland devised the "cracking snare drum rhythm" for "Every Breath You Take," an element considered arguably as important to the song's endurance as Sting's melody. "The guitar arpeggio, that famous smoldering riff which Andy Summers came up with himself and the cracking snare drum rhythm that Stuart Copeland devised."

podcast.body: His father, Miles Copeland Jr., was a part-time jazz musician and notably a founding member of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). podcast.title: Idea for The Police
podcast.body: In 1977, amidst the burgeoning punk scene in England, Stuart Copeland originated the idea to form a harder rocking power trio, which he intended to name "the police." "By 1977, Punk was exploded across England and Stuart Copeland had a notion to start a harder rocking power trio he wanted to call the police."

podcast.body: By 1977, after having played with Curved Air for two albums, Stuart Copeland had gained a reputation as a "gregarious drummer of both power and detail," which greatly impressed Sting. "As for Stuart, by 1977, he had been playing with Curved Air for two albums and earned a reputation as a gregarious drummer of both power and detail. Sting was impressed with him right away."

podcast.title: Unique Upbringing
podcast.body: Born in Virginia, outside Washington D.C., and raised in Cairo, Stuart Copeland had traveled the world due to his father's international work. "Even before he joined Curved Air, the London-based progressive rock group, Stuart Copeland led a unique life, born in Virginia just outside of Washington, D.C. and raised in Cairo."

xref.title: 1977 Breakthrough Sound
xref.body: When The Police emerged in 1977, Stuart Copeland's drumming immediately distinguished itself from other New Wave drummers of the era. His snare drum was tuned very tightly, producing a sharp, high-pitched crack, and his playing incorporated a distinct reggae and dub feel, often expressed with rim shots. There was also a subtle Middle Eastern infusion blended with jazz, evident in his use of small, high-pitched splash cymbals, making him one of the first modern rock drummers to adopt them. He was also notable for his syncopated beats led from the hi-hat. "When they came along in 1977, he immediately stood out from all the other new wave drummers of the era."

xref.title: Joined The Police at 36 (1977)
xref.body: In 1977, after years of working in various musical roles, Andy Summers, then 36, accepted an invitation to join Sting and Stuart Copeland in the newly forming band, The Police, breaking through the following year. "So after bouncing around for years in 1977, he accepted an invitation to join Sting and Stuart Copeland in the police, which was just starting out."

xref.title: Band Name Origin
xref.body: The band's name, The Police, was a direct reference to drummer Stuart Copeland's father, who was a former CIA agent. His father had been a senior black ops operative involved in sponsoring a coup in Syria in the 1940s. "Their name, the police, was a nod to the fact that drummer Stuart Copen's father was a former CIA agent."

xref.title: Drumming Influences
xref.body: Taylor Hawkins' drumming style was heavily influenced by progressive rock drummers such as Neil Peart of Rush, Stewart Copeland of The Police, and Phil Collins during his time with Genesis. Other influences included Stephen Perkins of Jane's Addiction, Ringo Starr, and his hero, Roger Taylor of Queen. "His heroes were Neil Pirate of Rush, Stuart Copeland of the police, and Phil Collins when he was with Genesis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Left-Handed on Right-Handed Kit
xref.body: Stuart Copeland is left-handed but plays a drum kit set up for right-handers, which made his complex rhythms even more distinctive. This playing style has been compared to Ringo Starr, who, despite playing right-handed, frequently led with his left hand for fills and flourishes. As a three-piece band, The Police's structure provided ample space for Stuart Copeland's elaborate drumming. "His rhythms were made all the more complicated because Stuart is left-handed."

xref.title: Snare Drum Sample for Peter Gabriel
xref.body: An old Police record provided the snare drum sound that was sampled for Peter Gabriel's "So" album. Stuart Copeland, although credited on the album, often only contributed this original snare sound, which was then digitally manipulated and used. "Stuart Copeland is credited with playing on the record, but all he really did was contribute the snare drum sound sampled from some old police record."
